_comment: Mutation survivors accepted as a baseline for the binding sweep (the membership walk, the context it carries, and the frontend). The nightly ratchet fails when a survivor appears outside this set, and when an entry is no longer a survivor. Regenerate with `python scripts/mutation_gate.py --baseline walk --update` after a sweep, and only ever let this set shrink. Entries are the survivor line without its line:col position, so they survive unrelated code motion.

_accepted.crates/valgebra-py/src/build/refine.rs:: `mask & (bit | HOOK) != 0` becomes `mask | (bit | HOOK) != 0`, which is true for every probe because a bit is never zero: the reading asks for every name, every time. The mask chooses between asking the interpreter for a name and not asking, and asking is what the frontend did before the mask existed: `getattr_opt` answers correctly for a name that is there and for one that is not. So a mutant of the mask can only move cost, which is `scripts/perf_gate.py --binding-annotated`'s business and not a test's. The direction that would matter -- skipping a name a marker really carries -- is not equivalent and is not excused: the corpus asks a marker of each shape a name can live in (a `slots` type, an instance dictionary, a `__getattr__` hook, and a type with both), and the mutants that skipped a carried name die on those rows. The file is `build/refine.rs` since the frontend's surfaces moved beside the dispatch; this baseline is keyed by path, so a mutant whose file moves reads as a new one until its key does too.

_accepted.crates/valgebra-py/src/check/index.rs: d: `if !fields.is_empty()` read as `if fields.is_empty()`: an attribute record with no fields gains a plan of no names, and one with fields gains none. Both halves are cost. A plan of no names is what a record of no fields would get anyway, and a record with fields falls back to its own text. The walk falls back for a schema the index does not carry -- every plan lookup in `check/walk/` is `Option`-shaped with the fallback written beside it -- so a traversal that skips a node decides the same values and only pays more for them.

The attribute plan, which holds each declared name interned. Without it `attr_record_matches` reads `field.name` and interns nothing, so every attribute lookup hashes the name rather than comparing a pointer -- the same answer from the same names. The walk falls back for a schema the index does not carry -- every plan lookup in `check/walk/` is `Option`-shaped with the fallback written beside it -- so a traversal that skips a node decides the same values and only pays more for them.

_accepted.crates/valgebra-py/src/check/index.rs: r: The traversal `__traverse__` hands the cycle collector. Every object it yields is an interned `str`, and a `str` refers to nothing, so it can be no edge of a cycle and a collector that never sees one still collects correctly. The method exists because a traversal omitting an owned reference is wrong on its own terms, not because this omission leaks: no test can distinguish the two, and none should be written to.
_accepted.crates/valgebra-py/src/check/walk.rs: de: Cannot change a verdict. The speculative sub-check inherits the caller's mode instead of the fast one, so a discarded branch walk aggregates into a throwaway buffer. Same answer, more work.

No test can kill it, so a count does. `scripts/perf_gate.py --binding-subclass` walks a three-field `NamedTuple`, and reading every subclass as a liar reads **+171.65%** there -- 121,700,049 instructions against 44,800,049. This is the reading both halves are written in: `reads_its_length` and `reads_its_elements` differ only in the slot they name, and the answer `false` here is the answer `false` from either of them.

This is the set half, asked of `__iter__`: a subclass is read through the base's iterator, which yields the same members the subclass holds. No shape of the instruction gate walks a set subclass, so the count above is the sequence half's and this one is argued rather than measured -- the two readings are the same three interpreter calls, one slot apart.

It was one function answering for both slots, named `reads_its_storage` and taking the slot as an argument, and the measurement above is of this same reading under that name; the argument the slot used to carry is now the two functions' names, which is what lets each say what it is for.
_accepted.crates/valgebra-py/src/check/walk/record: The closed record's classification. Without its arm a closed record reads as one whose clause must be read, and takes the scan: a closed record has no clause, so the scan refuses an undeclared key as the reading by keys does, and every answer is the same. What moves is the cost -- the scan resolves each key by name where the reading by keys probes each field -- and `scripts/perf_gate.py --binding-record` is the gate that holds it.

`plan.keys.len() != fields.len()` is a defensive refusal: the plan is built from the same field list and a caller cannot spell two fields with one name (the frontend rejects duplicates), so the counts are always equal and the guard never fires. Flipping it makes the guard always fire, which turns the fast path off and leaves the scan to answer -- the same equivalence as the switch above.

Cannot change a report. The counter it disables is what lets a closed record holding exactly its own keys skip a scan that would find nothing: stuck at zero, the count matches only an empty value, so every other record falls through to the scan and the scan reports what the count would have. Only the cost moves, and cost is the instruction budget's business. The other half of the same condition is not equivalent and is killed by tests/test_mutation.py: a value that grows while it is explained leaves the count matching entries it no longer has, which is why the length is read again before the skip is taken.

As above, from the other side: a counter stuck at zero leaves the loop terminated by the iterator alone, which exhausts after exactly the entries the dict held. A dict that changed size is caught by the length check before the iterator is advanced, and one that changed without changing size panics inside `next` whether or not the count moved. So the count is belt and braces over a bound the length check already holds, and no dict distinguishes them.

The entry count bounds the scan, and no dict can show the bound being loose by one. The extra turn the mutant allows re-checks the length, finds the iterator exhausted, and breaks -- the same answer, reached one step later. What the count is for is keeping the iterator away from the state PyO3 panics in, and the length check at the top of each turn is what actually reaches that state first, so the two cannot be told apart by a value. Driven both ways by hand: every Rust and Python test passes under the mutation.

The guard that keeps a record whose clause reads a key off the by-keys path. Inverted, such a record is read by its keys first and then, since its clause cannot be answered without the key, handed to the scan -- the answer the scan gives, at the cost of the reading before it -- while every other record goes straight to the scan. No answer moves; the two record shapes on the gate hold the cost.
The same guard on the JSON side, and the same argument: the counts agree by construction, so flipping the comparison retires the fast path and the document search answers instead.

The fast path's switch: `None` sends the walk to the scan it replaced, which decides the same values. `a_closed_record_answers_for_each_of_its_keys` holds the two to the same answers; the difference between them is the cost, and the sweep cannot read a cost.

The top clause's classification. Without it the top clause reads as one to be read, and a record open under it takes the scan, which asks the clause about each undeclared key and hears yes every time. Same answers; the cost is the scan's, and no binding shape carries the top clause -- the open shape carries the `TypedDict` clause, which is the one a frontend builds.

The `TypedDict` clause's classification. Without it every `TypedDict` value takes the scan, as it did before the reading by keys admitted it, and every answer is the same: the scan asks `str: anything` about each undeclared key and hears what the type test says. `scripts/perf_gate.py --binding-open` is the gate that holds it, at 29% of the shape.

The same guard, weakened rather than inverted: a record whose clause reads a key and whose plan is complete is read by its keys and then handed to the scan. Same answers, by the same fallback, and the same gate.
_accepted.crates/valgebra-py/src/check/walk/scalar: The fast path's switch. `None` means "this sequence is not one scalar kind", so the walk takes the general element loop -- which is the path this one was measured against and must agree with (`the_scalar_loop_and_the_walk_admit_the_same_values`). Turning it off changes no answer and costs 70% of a list of integers, and no test can see the difference in an answer, which is what makes it equivalent rather than untested.
_accepted.crates/valgebra-py/src/check/walk/sequen: The sibling of the accepted `scan_dict` entry, on the same loop and for the same reason. The element count bounds the scan, and no list can show the bound being loose by one: the extra turn the mutant allows re-checks the length, finds the iterator exhausted and breaks, which is the answer the post-loop check already gives. The iterator cannot yield an extra element either, because a list that grew is refused by the length check at the top of that turn before `next` is asked. Driven both ways by hand: the binding interpreter tests and the whole Python suite pass under the mutation, the resize rows included.

The condition tells a sequence whose C length is its storage from one whose is not: an exact tuple, or a subclass that inherits the base's `__len__`. Read as `&&`, only an exact tuple qualifies and every subclass is copied through the base slot -- which decides exactly the same things, because the copy holds the same elements. An answer-equivalent mutant, and it is the regression this condition was written to end: a `NamedTuple` cost 100 ns against a plain tuple's 57 while every test passed. No test can kill it, so a count does: `scripts/perf_gate.py --binding-subclass` walks a three-field `NamedTuple`, and reverting this line reads **+171.65%** there -- 121,700,049 instructions against 44,800,049.
